In `for i in f { a } {`, head-restriction refuses the reading whose head holds the trailing closure, and trailing-closure refuses the one that takes `{ a }` as the body and the next brace as a trailing closure on the loop; the grammar does not say which refusal a parser reports, and `for` has no other head to place it in.

In `for i in f { a }..x {`, the recognizer reads the loop `for i in f { a }` as the range's first operand and `x { }` as a call with a trailing closure; syntax.rule.block-tail says a loop that starts a statement is a statement, never an operand, but the recognizer does not apply block-tail, so that reading is not recorded and the refusal block-tail would make has no name to record until it does.

In `borrow let x = f { a } {`, head-restriction, trailing-closure and borrow-form each refuse another reading, and the grammar does not say which refusal a parser reports; a borrow block has no other head to place it in.

In `borrow let x = a.. {`, range-open-end refuses the block reading and borrow-form the unwrap reading, and the grammar does not say which refusal a parser reports; a borrow block has no other head to place it in.

The self-hosted lexer refuses a letter outside ASCII as an unexpected character, so the recognizer never sees an identifier holding one and never refuses a text by this name; the negative cases syntax.lex.ascii-identifier/* record that lexical refusal as a parse error.

The recognizer names borrow-form only by the `=` after `borrow let NAME` or `borrow var NAME`, refusing the place reading, which parses only while an operand follows the `=`; dropping the tokens after it changes the name, so every such case records parse-error (README, Refusals). Naming borrow-form at its token is a recognizer change, as SL-410 is for range-open-end.
